courseMetadata.title: Testing JavaScript with Jest
courseMetadata.description: A short, hands-on tour of the v6.1 runnable-code widgets — playgrounds, graded challenges, predictions, and an interactive Jest tutorial.

prerequisites.description: Comfortable writing JavaScript functions and using `const`/`let`.

competencies.title: Aggregating arrays
competencies.description: Collapse a list into a single value with reduce, including the empty case.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: reduce always starts from the first element, so the initial value is optional.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Without an initial value, `reduce` uses element 0 as the seed and starts at index 1. On an **empty** array that throws a TypeError, and on an array of objects it makes the accumulator an object rather than a number.

competencies.title: Writing Jest tests
competencies.description: Express behaviour as describe/it blocks and choose matchers that actually constrain the code.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the happy path passes, the function works.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A test suite is only as strong as its least convenient case. Empty inputs, boundaries and error paths are where real defects live.

sections.title: Running code, not reading it
sections.description: Every idea in this section is something you execute rather than take on faith.

learningObjectives.description: Predict and verify what a program prints.

motivationHooks.prompt: You have read that `reduce` collapses an array. Can you say, precisely, what it does when the array is empty?

sectionSummary.content: You should now believe three things: running code beats reading it, `reduce` needs an explicit seed to be safe, and a test that only covers the happy path is barely a test.
keyTakeaways: `reduce` without an initial value throws on an empty array
A prediction you committed to is worth more than one you didn't
Tests should include at least one case that could plausibly fail

contentBlocks.content:
## Start by running something

The fastest way to understand `reduce` is to watch it work. The block below is live — press **Run** and see.

contentBlocks.caption: A read-only example you can still execute.

contentBlocks.title: The seed is the whole story
contentBlocks.content: That `0` at the end is the **initial accumulator**. Drop it and `reduce` quietly changes behaviour: it uses element 0 as the seed and begins at index 1.
Try it yourself. Remove the `, 0` below and run it against an empty array.

contentBlocks.caption: Scratch space — nothing here is graded.

interactionSequence.prompt: Read this carefully. **What exactly does it print?** Commit to an answer before you run it.

codeExercise.explanation: `ys = xs` copies the **reference**, not the array. There is only one array here, and both names point at it. This is the single most common source of "but I never touched that variable" bugs.

interactionSequence.prompt:
Implement `total` so it returns the sum of every item's `price`.

It must return `0` for an empty list.

codeExercise.solutionNote: The seed `0` is what makes the empty case work.

hints: `reduce` takes a callback and an initial value.
Start the accumulator at `0` so an empty list has an answer.
feedback.elaborativeFeedback: `reduce` with an explicit seed is total: it has a defined answer for every input, including the empty array.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How sure are you before checking?

interactionSequence.prompt: Print a countdown from `3` to `1`, one number per line.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Why does `reduce` need an initial value to be safe?

contentBlocks.content:
## The grammar of a Jest test

A Jest suite is three nested ideas:

- `describe(name, fn)` groups related tests
- `it(name, fn)` is one behaviour you claim is true
- `expect(value).toBe(other)` is the claim itself

Everything else is detail.

contentBlocks.title: About this environment
contentBlocks.content: These exercises run against a **Jest-compatible subset** built into the course player, not Jest itself. `describe`, `it`, `expect`, the common matchers, the `beforeEach`/`afterEach` hooks and `jest.fn()` all behave as they do in Jest. Module mocking, snapshots and the CLI are out of scope here.

contentBlocks.caption: A complete, passing suite. Run it.

workedExamples.title: From behaviour to assertion
workedExamples.problem: You are handed `slugify(s)` and asked to prove it works.
steps: Name the behaviour out loud: "it lowercases the text".
Turn that sentence into an `it(...)` title, unchanged.
Write the smallest `expect` that would fail if the behaviour broke.
workedExamples.conclusion: A good test title is a sentence about behaviour. If you cannot write the sentence, you do not yet know what you are testing.

interactionSequence.prompt:
`slugify` is already written. **Write the tests.**

You need at least three `it(...)` blocks, and they all have to pass. Think about whitespace and about input that is already a slug.

codeExercise.solutionNote: Four tests, each one a sentence about behaviour.

hints: What should `slugify('hello world')` return? Assert it.
Try a string with several spaces in a row.
What about leading and trailing whitespace?
feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Notice that you never changed `slugify`. Tests are a description of behaviour you can execute.

interactionSequence.prompt: Now the other direction. The tests are written for you and they are **failing**. Fix `capitalize` until they pass.

hints: Guard the empty string before you index into it.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: what makes a test suite weak, even when every test in it passes?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A suite is weak when its cases could not plausibly fail — when it only exercises the path the author already had in mind.

transferExercises.scenario: You inherit a function with no tests and no documentation.
transferExercises.task: Write three test titles — just the sentences, no code — that would tell the next reader what the function guarantees.
successCriteria: Each title describes behaviour, not implementation
At least one covers an edge case
None of them mention internal variable names

questions.prompt: What does `[].reduce((a, b) => a + b)` do?
questions.reviewPromptOverride: What happens when you reduce an empty array with no initial value?

optionFeedback.feedback: That is what happens *with* an initial value of `0`.
Correct — with no seed and nothing to seed from, there is no answer to give.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the strongest test?

optionFeedback.feedback: The empty case is the one most likely to be wrong, so it carries the most information.
`toBeTruthy` passes for `3`, `'banana'` and `[]` alike — it barely constrains anything.

glossary.definition: The running value `reduce` carries from one element to the next.
The assertion method chained onto `expect(...)`, such as `toBe` or `toEqual`.
